title: Manifest checksum/timestamp desync — incident recap
content:
Summary:
During a staged model rollout on 2024-11-03 we observed intermittent decoding anomalies and token ID shifts on ~12% of canary hosts, triggered during a metadata-driven weight swap. The canary health checks passed basic liveness but downstream decode checks (sample prompts) returned shifted tokens or missing EOS on affected hosts. The surface impact: slow degradation in generation quality for the canary cohort, fast detection by eval probes, and automatic rollback to previous model version before customer-facing impact.

High level timeline (local times):
- 08:12 deploy pipeline triggered: new model manifest pushed to model-registry (manifest id m-20241103-7).
- 08:13 object-store completed shard uploads (shard-sets s-77x).
- 08:14 registry updated manifest checksum (sha256: abcd...), but object-store replication timestamp lagged for a subset of regions due to backend maintenance window.
- 08:14:30 rollout agent (fast-path enabled) evaluated manifest freshness using the storage object timestamp heuristic and decided no re-fetch was needed on hosts where timestamp was older though checksum was newer.
- 08:15 first canary host reported stray decode tokens during sample prompt eval.
- 08:17 canary health checker flagged 3/25 hosts as degraded (tokenization mismatch).
- 08:20 mitigations applied: rollout paused, forced revalidation initiated for all canary hosts.
- 08:28 forced re-pulls completed with checksum verification, and affected hosts recovered.
- 08:35 rollback to prior manifest completed for full fleet pending further investigation.

What happened (investigation summary):
The rollout agent uses a two-step metadata sanity check to decide whether to avoid re-downloading model shards to minimize reload time: 1) compare manifest timestamp on object-store vs local, 2) if timestamp newer then fetch; otherwise fast-path no-op. This optimization assumed strong timestamp monotonicity across storage replication. During a recent storage maintenance window, object-store replication timestamps were temporarily inconsistent: the model-registry updated the manifest checksum immediately, but the object metadata timestamp visible to some regions lagged. The rollout agent saw the older timestamp and skipped re-fetch on a subset of hosts, resulting in a hybrid state where new manifest pointers (e.g., tokenizer variant id) were used while actual weight shards remained the pre-rollout versions. That mixed state caused subtle token ID mappings to diverge on affected hosts.

Root cause (short):
- Primary: rollout fast-path relied on storage timestamp as authoritative and did not require checksum equality for the decision to skip re-fetch (race between checksum propagation and timestamp replication).
- Secondary: canary probes did not include a deterministic token-id/decoding sanity test until after the health regressions started.
- Tertiary: KV cache flush/validation was not part of the forced revalidation flow, which prolonged recovery on some hosts that kept stale KV entries.

Why it only affected a subset of hosts:
- Object-store metadata replication was regionally delayed; hosts in those regions saw older timestamps and took the fast-path skip.
- Some hosts had already evicted relevant KV caches and therefore re-applied correct token mappings after partial weight merges; others retained stale cache entries and exhibited persistent mismatch until forced flush/restart.

Immediate mitigations performed (what we did):
- Paused rollout within 5 minutes of detection.
- Forced full checksum validation and shard re-fetch on all canary hosts (agent command: agentctl model validate --manifest m-20241103-7 --force).
- Flushed KV caches on affected hosts and restarted the local inference worker for clean state.
- Rolled back the global rollout to the prior manifest to prevent wider exposure while we investigated (rollback id: m-20241029-3).
- Opened SRE-821 and MODEL-4523 to track follow-ups and telemetry additions.

Recovery notes:
- Revalidation + KV flush fixed 100% of previously affected hosts; decoding tests passed after re-pulls.
- Rollback prevented customer-facing impact; no SLA breach.
- Some hosts required two restarts because an unflushed disk-based KV persisted between soft restarts; we documented the path in the ticket.

Longer-term fixes (action items):
1) Rollout agent change: change fast-path decision to require checksum equality (manifest etag) in addition to timestamp. If checksum mismatch or unknown, force fetch. (Owner: Ethan Park, PR: serving-runtime#1428).
2) Add a pre-rollout deterministic decode test into the canary gate: run fixed prompts and verify token ids/EOS/length for a tiny set of examples to detect tokenizer/weight mismatches earlier. (Owner: Mariela Ortiz).
3) Add explicit metadata propagation telemetry: metric that tracks manifest checksum vs visible object timestamp divergence by region; alert if divergence > 30s. (Owner: SRE-Metrics).
4) KV cache hard-flush step: include an explicit KV invalidation in forced revalidation flow and document soft vs hard restart paths. (Owner: Jonah Li).
5) Update rollout playbook to include explicit storage maintenance gating and a temporary disable of the timestamp fast-path during known replication windows. (Owner: eng-release).
6) Add integration test that simulates out-of-order metadata updates (checksum arrives before timestamp) and validates the rollout agent behavior. (Owner: infra-test).
7) Postmortem writeup and exec summary for GTM (short version for execs to confirm no customer impact). (Owner: Aisha Kumar).

Open questions / follow-up investigation threads:
- Why did the object-store replication choose to propagate checksum before updating the visible object timestamp in some regions? (Storage vendor ops engaged, storage-ops ticket created).
- Is there any scenario where checksum equality check could be expensive at scale (e.g., too many objects)? Explore etag vs full checksum tradeoffs.
- Should we adopt a model manifest signed snapshot that includes both timestamp and checksum atomically (single source of truth) stored in the model-registry?

Runbook edits (draft notes):
- New step: when pause is triggered for metadata mismatch, run: agentctl model validate --manifest <id> --force-checksum and agentctl kv flush --pattern model:<id> --hard.
- Canary gate: include script canary-decode-check.sh that returns non-zero on token-id mismatch. Place this in serving-runtime tests and as an on-host gate.
- Add a quick reference: if affected-hosts > 5% during canary, rollback immediately and do forced pull + kv flush; if < 5%, pause and do targeted revalidate followed by full roll-forward.

Notes to SRE oncall (practical commands observed to help):
- agentctl model status --host <host> (shows manifest pointer + checksum + local shard ids)
- agentctl model validate --manifest <id> --force (trigger re-fetch and checksum verification)
- agentctl kv status --pattern model:<id> (list kv entries)
- agentctl kv flush --pattern model:<id> --hard (hard flush persistent and in-memory kv)
- systemctl restart inference-worker (when soft restart insufficient)

Unresolved items captured in tickets:
- SRE-821: telemetry/alert for checksum/timestamp divergence; post-incident storage vendor RCA attachment.
- MODEL-4523: rollout-agent code change PR + integration regression tests.
- infra-1172: storage replication test harness and simulation.

Appendix / artifacts collected:
- agent logs (canary hosts): /var/log/agent/canary-20241103-*.log (archived to S3 under s3://redwood-incident-archives/2024-11-03-manifest-desync).
- sample failing decode traces and token-id diffs attached to MODEL-4523.
- storage vendor timeline and customer support exchange attached in SRE-821.

Quick lessons learned (TL;DR):
- Do not trust timestamps alone for metadata freshness in geographically replicated object stores.
- Canary gates must include deterministic correctness checks (token-id/decode) beyond simple latency/liveness.
- KV caches complicate recovery; make hard flush cheap and reliable.

This doc is a working investigation — please add notes, expand the runbook steps, and flag any missed fallout. If you touched deployment code in the last 72 hours, paste commit ids here for correlation.

Recent commits referenced during debugging:
- serving-runtime: commit 6f3b2d3 - add fast-path timestamp heuristic (2024-09-12)
- registry: commit 2a9f4a1 - manifest checksum calc change (2024-10-29)

Next sync: 2024-11-11 09:00 (postmortem + rollout-agent PR review).
